subject: History
source: National Curriculum KS1 (events beyond living memory: the Great Fire of London, 1666); no school Drive history material found for Y2, written from scratch | Spring 2 2027: TGA Year 2 pack, Topic, Towers, Tunnels & Turrets (castles, Brunel, review)

lessons.unit: Unit 1: The Great Fire of London
lessons.title: London in 1666
objectives: Say when and where the Great Fire of London happened
Describe what London was like in 1666

keywords.def: the capital city of England
the year of the Great Fire, over 350 years ago
wood used for building
not wide

starter: What is the difference between past and present?
Name one old toy from our Year 1 work.

teach.heading: Bismillah: a story from long ago
teach.note: Say bismillah. Explain that this is an event before anyone alive today was born, so we find out from clues. Show 1666 on a timeline next to today.

teach.heading: Where is London?
bullets: The River Thames flows through it
teach.note: Show a simple map of the UK with London marked. Pupils may live in or near London; ask who has visited. Check they know the Thames is a river.

teach.heading: Houses in 1666
bullets: Most houses were made of wood
Roofs were covered in thatch or pitch
Streets were narrow and houses close together
teach.note: Show a picture of a Tudor or Stuart street with houses leaning over the road. Ask: what would happen if one house caught fire? Introduce 'timber' and 'narrow'.

teach.heading: Fire dangers
bullets: Homes used candles and open fires
The summer of 1666 was very dry
teach.note: Keep it simple. Explain that dry wood burns easily, so London was in danger. Do not frighten pupils; stress that nobody wanted a fire and that people later learned from it.

practice: Was London built of wood or stone in 1666?
Why were the narrow streets a problem?
Find London on the map of England.
independent: Draw a house in 1666 with wooden walls
Label wood, narrow street and chimney
exit: What was most London housing made of in 1666?
lessons.homework: Find London on a map or globe at home and show a grown-up where it is.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: label cards with pictures for wood, street, river. Stretch: explain why wooden houses caught fire easily.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: The Great Fire of London
lessons.title: How the fire started and spread
objectives: Say where and when the fire started
Explain why the fire spread so quickly

keywords.def: a place where bread is baked
the street in London where the fire started
to move across a bigger area
a book where someone writes about each day

starter: In which year was the Great Fire of London?
What were most houses made of?
Name the river that flows through London.

teach.heading: The fire begins
bullets: It began in a bakery in Pudding Lane
teach.note: The fire started in the early hours of Sunday morning, in the bakery of Thomas Farriner, the King's baker. Use the phrase 'in the night' to help pupils sequence.

teach.heading: Why it spread
bullets: A strong wind blew the flames
teach.note: Link directly to lesson 1. Ask pupils to give the three reasons using 'because'. Mention the wind came from the east and pushed the fire across the city.

teach.heading: Samuel Pepys' diary
bullets: He saw the fire from his window
His diary is a clue for us
teach.note: Samuel Pepys worked for the Navy and wrote a famous diary. He buried his cheese and his office papers to save them, which pupils often enjoy. Explain that a diary is a primary source: it was written by someone who was there.

teach.heading: Four days of fire
bullets: The fire burned for four days
Much of the old city was destroyed
teach.note: Count the days on a calendar: Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday. About 13,200 houses and 87 churches were destroyed. Keep numbers approximate.

practice: Give one reason why the fire spread quickly. Use because.
Who wrote a diary about the fire?
independent: Draw the fire starting in Pudding Lane
Put these in order: the fire starts, the fire spreads, the fire ends
exit: On which day did the Great Fire start?
Why is Pepys' diary useful to historians?
lessons.homework: Tell someone at home the three reasons why the fire spread quickly.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: sentence frame 'The fire spread because the houses were ...'. Stretch: write two reasons joined with 'and'.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: The Great Fire of London
lessons.title: Fighting the fire
objectives: Describe how people tried to stop the fire

keywords.def: a container for carrying water
a gap made so a fire cannot spread across it
a person trained to put out fires
the male ruler of a country

starter: Where did the Great Fire start?
Name one reason the fire spread.
Who wrote a famous diary about the fire?

teach.heading: No fire engines
bullets: There was no fire brigade in 1666
People used leather buckets of water
Some used long hooks to pull houses down
teach.note: Show pictures of leather buckets and fire hooks. Ask: how is this different from a fire engine today? Pupils compare old and new.

teach.heading: Making a firebreak
bullets: People pulled down houses in the fire's path
A gap with nothing to burn stops flames
teach.note: Use a simple demonstration: a line of paper houses on screen, remove the middle two. Show that the flames cannot jump a gap easily. Strong winds still made this difficult.

teach.heading: The King helps
bullets: King Charles II came to help
teach.note: The King and the Duke of York joined the fire fighting. Mention people from all parts of society worked together, which fits our value of helping others.

teach.heading: Then and now
bullets: Now: fire engines, hoses and hydrants
Now: smoke alarms warn us early
teach.note: Make a quick then/now chart. Add a safety message: smoke alarms, never play with matches, know how to leave your home safely.

practice: What did people use to carry water in 1666?
Name one thing firefighters use today.
independent: Draw firefighting equipment from 1666 (leather bucket, fire hook, squirt) and a fire engine today
Write two things that are the same or different
Write one safety rule for fires
exit: Name one thing used to fight the fire in 1666.
Name one thing used to fight fires today.
lessons.homework: Ask a grown-up where the smoke alarm is in your home and how you would leave safely.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use picture cards for bucket, hook, hose. Stretch: explain why a firebreak is useful.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: The Great Fire of London
lessons.title: After the fire: rebuilding London
objectives: Explain what changed after the Great Fire
Say who Sir Christopher Wren was

keywords.def: to build again
a hard block used to build walls
a person who designs buildings
a tall column in London that remembers the fire

starter: What did people use to fight the fire?
Which king helped fight the fire?

teach.heading: What was lost?
bullets: Many people had to find new homes
teach.note: Begin with bismillah and a short dua of thanks for safety. Be sensitive: officially only a few deaths were recorded, but many people lost their homes and belongings. Avoid over-dramatic detail.

teach.heading: A safer London
bullets: New houses were built of brick and stone
New laws said houses must be brick or stone
teach.note: Link to why the fire spread: ask pupils what they would change. They should suggest bricks, wide roads, no wood. Praise the cause-and-effect thinking.

teach.heading: Sir Christopher Wren
bullets: He designed a new St Paul's Cathedral
He also designed many other churches
teach.note: Show St Paul's Cathedral. Say the new cathedral took many years to finish. Define 'architect' as someone who plans buildings.

teach.heading: Remembering the fire
bullets: The Monument was built near Pudding Lane
It is a tall stone column
It reminds us of the fire
teach.note: Show a picture of the Monument. It is about 61 metres tall (202 feet) and stands near where the fire began. Ask: why do people build monuments?

practice: What new materials were used to build houses after the fire?
Who designed the new St Paul's Cathedral?
Why did people build wider streets?
independent: Draw London after the fire with brick houses and wide streets
Write two ways London changed after the fire
Draw the Monument and write one fact about it
exit: Name one thing that changed after the Great Fire.
Why did people build the Monument?
lessons.homework: Draw or build a brick house from bricks, paper or blocks and say why it is safer than a wooden house.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: word bank (brick, wide, stone, cathedral). Stretch: write a 'before and after' sentence for London.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Castles and Isambard Kingdom Brunel (Towers, Tunnels & Turrets)
lessons.title: What is a castle?
lessons.bigQuestion: Why would anyone build a home with walls this thick?
objectives: To understand what castles are and why people built them long ago
successCriteria: All: say what a castle is
Most: give one reason castles were built
Some: put castles on a timeline before today
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: ordering numbers on a timeline
lessons.smsc: Cultural: the history of Britain's buildings

keywords.def: a big, strong building with thick walls, built long ago
a very long time before we were born
a line that shows things in time order
keep safe
people from France who took over England in 1066

hook.text: If you had to keep your family safe long ago, what would you build?

starter.q: Wood, metal and plastic are all ...
A material that lets water soak in is:
Name one thing that rots in soil.
starter.a: For example: fruit peel or paper

teach.heading: What is a castle?
teach.note: Show a photo of a real castle. Ask: what do you notice?

teach.heading: Why build castles?
bullets: To show who was in charge
teach.note: After 1066 the Normans built many castles to control England.

teach.heading: Castles on a timeline
teach.note: The Tower of London was begun nearly a thousand years ago.

timeline.label: About 1078
timeline.text: The White Tower in London is begun
Conwy Castle in Wales is begun

timeline.label: Today
timeline.text: We visit castles and learn from them

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.why: Most castles in Britain were built hundreds of years ago.

practice.q: Why did people build thick walls?
practice.a: To keep people safe from attack
practice.model:
Thick walls are hard to break.
Enemies cannot get in.
People inside are safe.
So thick walls protect people.

practice.q: Who built many castles in England after 1066?
Is 1066 long ago or last week?

independent.q: Core: Draw a castle and write one sentence: 'Castles were built to ...'
independent.a: For example: Castles were built to keep people safe
independent.model: Teacher draws a tower and walls first and writes the sentence.

independent.q: Extend: Put three cards in time order: 1066, about 1078, today.
Stretch: Give a second reason castles were built.
independent.a: For example: to guard land or show who was in charge

exit.q: Big question: why build a home with thick walls?
exit.a: To keep people safe and keep enemies out

lessons.homework: Look at photos of a castle online with an adult and find its towers and walls.
lessons.send: SEND: castle picture with labels to trace. EAL: castle, wall, tower, safe with pictures. Stretch: find one castle near where you live on a map.

objectives: To understand how each part of a castle helped to keep it safe
successCriteria: All: name three parts of a castle

lessons.smsc: Social: working together to keep a community safe

keywords.def: the strongest tower, in the middle
a ditch of water round a castle
a bridge that can be pulled up
a heavy gate that drops down
a small tower
the top of a wall with gaps

hook.text: If you were guarding a castle, where would you stand to see enemies coming?

starter.q: Give one reason castles were built.
starter.a: To keep people safe (or guard the land)

teach.heading: Outside
bullets: Drawbridge: pulled up when danger came
teach.note: Show a real moat photo. Ask: how would you cross?

teach.heading: Gate and walls
teach.note: Guards could look out from turrets and battlements.

teach.heading: The keep
teach.note: Label a castle together.

steps: Find the water round the castle

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: A heavy gate that drops down is a:
check.why: A portcullis drops down to block the gate. A moat is water; a turret is a small tower.

practice.q: What is the water round a castle called?
practice.model:
I see water round the castle.
Water round a castle is a moat.
It is hard to cross.
It is a moat.

practice.q: What could be pulled up when enemies came?
Where were guards to look out?

independent.q: Core: Label six parts on the castle picture: keep, moat, drawbridge, portcullis, turret, battlements.
independent.model: Teacher labels 'moat' first with a straight line.

independent.q: Extend: Write how the moat kept people safe.
independent.a: For example: enemies could not walk up to the walls

independent.q: Stretch: Which part would you add to make it safer?

exit.q: The strongest tower in the middle is the:
Big question: which part would be hardest to get past?
exit.a: Any part with a reason, for example the moat, because you have to swim

lessons.send: SEND: label stickers; point and say. EAL: castle words with pictures. Stretch: add arrow slits and explain them.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Castles and Isambard Kingdom Brunel (Towers, Tunnels & Turrets)
lessons.title: Life in a castle
lessons.bigQuestion: Would you rather be the cook or the guard in a castle?
objectives: To understand who lived and worked in a castle and what their jobs were
successCriteria: All: name two jobs in a castle
Most: match a job to a room
Some: compare castle life with life today
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: materials for heat and light
lessons.smsc: Social: every job helps a community

keywords.def: the owner of the castle
a soldier who fought on a horse
someone who works for others
the big room for meals and meetings
someone who makes things from metal

hook.text: What jobs would be needed to look after a castle with hundreds of people?

starter.q: Water round a castle is a:
Name one part of a castle.
starter.a: Keep, moat, drawbridge, portcullis, turret or battlements

teach.heading: Who lived there?
teach.note: Explain each job. Show rooms and objects only, not people.

teach.heading: Jobs in a castle
teach.note: Who made horseshoes? The blacksmith.

teach.heading: Then and now
bullets: Then: fires for heat, candles for light
teach.note: Ask: what would you miss most?

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.why: The blacksmith heated metal in a forge to make tools, nails and horseshoes.

practice.model:
A cook makes food.
Food is made in the kitchen.
So the cook worked in the kitchen.

practice.q: How did people light rooms at night?

independent.q: Core: Match four jobs to four places on the sheet.
independent.a: Cook: kitchen; blacksmith: forge; guard: walls; steward: great hall

independent.q: Extend: Write one way castle life was different from now.
independent.a: For example: they used candles, we use electric lights

independent.q: Stretch: Which job would you choose and why?

lessons.homework: Tell your family about three castle jobs and which you would choose.

lessons.bigQuestion: How do you build a tunnel under a river without the water getting in?
objectives: To understand why Isambard Kingdom Brunel is remembered as a great engineer
successCriteria: All: name one thing Brunel built
Most: say what a bridge, tunnel and railway are for

lessons.crossCurricular: Design and technology: our paper bridge test
lessons.smsc: Moral: patience and hard work to solve problems

keywords.def: a person who designs and builds things
a way through or under the ground
something that crosses a river or a valley
a track for trains
a bridge that hangs from strong cables

hook.text: Which would be harder to build: a bridge over a river or a tunnel under it? Why?

starter.q: Who made things from metal in a castle?
Water round a castle is a:

teach.heading: Who was Brunel?
bullets: Built bridges, tunnels, railways and ships
teach.note: We look at what he built (photos of buildings, not people).

teach.heading: Tunnel and bridge
bullets: Thames Tunnel under the river, opened 1843
teach.note: He worked on the Thames Tunnel with his father. The bridge was finished after he died.

teach.heading: Railway and ships
bullets: Great Western Railway: London to Bristol
A big iron ship with a propeller
teach.note: His railway made journeys much faster.

timeline.text: Thames Tunnel opens; SS Great Britain launched

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.why: He designed and built bridges, tunnels, railways and ships.

practice.a: To go under a river or through a hill
practice.model:
A river is in the way.
We dig under it.
Now we can cross under the river.
That is a tunnel.

practice.q: Which two cities did his railway join?

independent.q: Core: Fill in the Brunel fact sheet: born, died, two things he built.
independent.a: Born 1806, died 1859; for example the Clifton Suspension Bridge and the Great Western Railway

independent.q: Extend: Write why his railway helped people.
independent.a: Journeys were faster, so people and goods travelled quickly

independent.q: Stretch: Which of his works is used today?
independent.a: The bridge, the tunnel and the railway are still used

exit.q: Big question: how do you build a tunnel without water getting in?
exit.a: Build strong walls and dig carefully under the river, as Brunel's team did
